strengths: Novel inversion-free paradigm for video editing that addresses fundamental limitations of prior methods; first application of flow-based inversion-free editing to native T2V models
Strong empirical results on key metrics: CLIP-T (33.84×10⁻²), CLIP-F (97.85×10⁻²), Frame-Acc (84.55%), outperforming multiple strong baselines across diverse editing scenarios
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 6 metrics, extensive qualitative results, ablation studies validating SAFC and DAG, and detailed appendix with implementation details
Practical efficiency improvements: DAG achieves 5.8× speedup over naive averaging (5 vs. 29 minutes for 41-frame video); training-free approach usable with pre-trained models
Well-motivated technical approach with clear problem articulation; honest discussion of limitations in Section F rather than overstating capabilities
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty: core approach applies established techniques (Flow Matching, CFG) to video with relatively straightforward extensions; SAFC is simple masking, DAG is unsurprising CFG extension; conceptually incremental over FlowEdit [24]

Significant practical limitations acknowledged but not addressed: method fails substantially when target prompt incompletely replaces source terms (Figure 8); explicitly limited performance on style transfer; restricts scope of editing applications

WarpSSIM performance gap unexplained: method achieves lowest structural fidelity scores (55.67×10⁻²) vs. baselines (60-78×10⁻²), contradicting structure-preservation claims; dismissal as 'over-editing capability' is somewhat circular without deeper analysis

Weak theoretical justification: claims that ODE paths preserve structure better than inversion lack rigorous support; noise cancellation argument oversimplified; no formal analysis of spatiotemporal manifold proximity; intuitive but not mathematically rigorous

Insufficient design ablation: choice of union masking operation unexplained; block selection (18th DiT) appears ad-hoc; hyperparameters (CFG scales 3.5/10.5, DAG weight 2.75) appear tuned to Wan 2.1 with unclear generalization to other T2V models

Evaluation gaps limiting confidence: no user studies to validate perceptual quality claims; implicit small test set with no size statistics; CLIP-based metrics have known temporal coherence limitations; failure mode analysis limited to Figure 8
Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable at review; mask generation involves multiple thresholds potentially requiring per-video tuning; hyperparameter sensitivity not systematically studied

Computational claims are relative: 5 minutes for 41 frames on four 4090 GPUs is still slow; single-GPU efficiency unreported; efficiency gains relative only to naive multi-round averaging, not to other state-of-the-art methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of inversion-based video editing methods with clear articulation of challenges
Non-intrusive SAFC design that operates externally to pre-trained models, improving generalizability compared to methods modifying internal model computations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (CLIP-T, CLIP-F, WarpSSIM, Qedit, PickScore, Frame-Acc) and extensive qualitative results across diverse editing scenarios
Solid technical execution with well-designed ODE formulation and shared noise instantiation to isolate semantic changes from noise effects
Ablation studies demonstrating contributions of individual components (SAFC and DAG)
Extensive supplementary materials including detailed experimental settings and algorithm pseudocode
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: ODE-based editing directly adapted from FlowEdit [24], SAFC is incremental attention masking, DAG is minor variant of Classifier-Free Guidance—primarily engineering-focused rather than conceptually novel

Critical unresolved practical limitation: Incomplete text replacement causes substantial editing failures (Figure 8); if target prompt retains any mention of original objects, method fails significantly, severely restricting real-world applicability
Single T2V model evaluation: All experiments use only Wan 2.1; no evaluation on ModelScope, MagicVideo, or other architectures despite claims of generality and adaptability
Weak baseline comparisons: Most baselines are T2I-adapted methods; only VideoDirector [48] is T2V-based; missing recent T2V-based methods (2024-2025), limiting impact assessment

Structure preservation contradiction: Achieves lowest WarpSSIM scores (57.69 vs. 68.14-72.64 for baselines) despite claiming to preserve structure—defensive explanation about 'pronounced deformations' undermines core motivation

Extensive unjustified hyperparameter tuning: 10-step skip (no ablation), window size 11, decay 0.25, asymmetric CFG scales (3.5 vs. 10.5), DAG weight 2.75, L_HQ=4, L_BL=2—appears cherry-picked with heavy overfitting to evaluation set

DAG methodology concerns: K=C(L_HQ,L_BL) grows exponentially; claimed 'negligible overhead' contradicted by 29min→5min speedup; mathematical justification for differential signals weak; unclear why this approach outperforms direct averaging
Acknowledged but unaddressed limitations: Style transfer performance 'relatively limited'; dependence on text quality and completeness; no solutions proposed for any limitations

Incomplete evaluation scope: Fixed at 50 denoising steps (40 effective) with no step-count sensitivity analysis; fixed resolution (832×480); limited frames (8-36); computational cost not analyzed in main paper; no inference time comparisons

Missing evaluation rigor: No perceptual user studies despite relying on automatic metrics; WarpSSIM measured via optical flow (RAFT) which fails on heavily edited content; PickScore trained on images not video; Frame-Acc is binary and coarse

Methodological issues: Equation 2 assumes temporal correspondence that may fail with large motion; single block selection (18th DiT) is model-specific; mask generation via cross-attention is brittle with no robustness analysis

Reproducibility concerns: Method depends on Wan 2.1 specific architecture; multiple model-specific design choices; hyperparameter sensitivity suggests limited transferability across models and settings
Overstated claims: 'State-of-the-art' claim not uniformly supported (WarpSSIM significantly worse); contradicts structure preservation claims by achieving worst performance on structure metrics

Missing comparisons and analysis: No cross-model generalization study; limited failure mode discussion; no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters; shallow justification for design choices throughout

strengths: First application of inversion-free editing paradigm to video editing with T2V models, addressing real limitations of inversion-based methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics and strong performance: outperforms baselines on CLIP-T (33.72 vs 32.93), CLIP-F (98.37 vs 97.13), Frame-Acc (84.38 vs 77.82), and achieves best Qedit
Well-motivated technical approach with elegant noise-cancellation mechanism through shared noise instances between source and target velocities
Non-intrusive SAFC design that operates externally to model architecture, enhancing generality and adaptability across different T2V models
Extensive qualitative validation with diverse editing scenarios (Figures 9-16) demonstrating practical effectiveness across object editing, texture transformation, and attribute modification
Significant computational efficiency gains: DAG achieves comparable results in 5 minutes versus 29 minutes for conventional averaging on 41-frame videos
Training-free approach with promised code release providing immediate practical value
Honest discussion of limitations including text replacement sensitivity and style transfer constraints
Reasonable ablation studies demonstrating contribution of SAFC and DAG components
weaknesses: Critical structural preservation trade-off: achieves lowest WarpSSIM score (57.69) versus best baseline (72.64), indicating substantial loss of structural fidelity despite claims of structure preservation

Severe practical limitation from text prompt dependency: method fails significantly when source prompt descriptions persist in target prompt (Appendix F), limiting usability without explicit prompt engineering guidance
Generalization concerns: all experiments exclusively on Wan 2.1 model; cross-attention extraction requires model-specific tuning; unclear how SAFC adapts to different attention architectures
Limited technical novelty: core ODE editing adapted from concurrent FlowEdit [24], SAFC applies established attention-guided masking, DAG uses standard CFG principles differentially

Insufficient ablation and hyperparameter analysis: introduces multiple parameters (L_HQ, L_BL, w, smoothing kernel n, decay factor δ) without sensitivity studies, justification, or comprehensive ablations

Theoretical justification gaps: velocity field averaging principle lacks rigorous analysis, validity of constructed Z_tar as true target intermediate state not formally established, mask generation heuristics (smoothing + thresholding) lack principled foundation

Narrow evaluation scope: single T2V model tested, relatively simple video scenarios, maximum 36 frames, no user studies, computational cost comparisons with baselines absent, long-video scalability unclear

Reproducibility limitations: architecture-dependent cross-attention extraction, implementation details scattered across appendices, no guidance for adapting to new models, potential brittleness of heuristic thresholds
Incomplete ablations: single SAFC example (Figure 5), no analysis of averaging sample count sensitivity, no investigation of failure modes beyond text replacement
